title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without the rights holders' authorization. Udio's AI music generator was alleged to have ingested protected recordings, including commercially released songs, to learn how to produce new music. This is a training-data sourcing problem, occurring before the model was ever deployed to users, meaning the legal and rights exposure was baked in from the start.

The incident produced multiple legal tracks simultaneously: settlements with Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group that included licensing arrangements, a new lawsuit from Sony Music alleging unauthorized use of more than 30,000 recordings, a surviving copyright class action brought by independent artists, and a separate lawsuit from a musicians' union over the UMG deal itself. A court declined to let Sony add those 30,000 recordings to its original case, prompting Sony to file a new action instead. That layered litigation shows how a single training-data decision can generate disputes across different rights holders, different legal theories, and different jurisdictions at once.

What is not established is whether any court has issued a final finding of infringement, whether Udio acted with knowledge that the training data was unlicensed, or what the precise terms of any settlement are, as financial details were not disclosed. The lawsuits are allegations, and the settlements do not constitute admissions of liability.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The settlement includes licensing agreements between the two companies. UMG and other major record labels had sued Udio for allegedly using hit songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission to create similar AI-generated music. Under the new deal, Udio will launch a platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, create, stream and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed.

This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label and represents a shift in how the AI music industry may operate going forward. Udio CEO Andrew Sanchez stated the collaboration demonstrates how AI and the music industry can work together to support artists. Artists can choose to participate in the new platform and will receive compensation, though specific details were not provided. Udio, which launched in 2024 and has been used by millions of people, was co-founded by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by notable investors including will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
